explain.say: Petrol and diesel engines both burn fuel in cylinders to push pistons, but they light the fuel in different ways, and that changes how they behave.

explain.say: A petrol engine mixes fuel with air, squeezes it to about a tenth of its volume and lights it with an electric spark from a spark plug. It is light, revs freely and runs smoothly.

explain.say: A diesel has no spark plugs. It squeezes air much harder, to about a fifteenth or twentieth of its volume, which makes it hot enough to light the fuel sprayed in. The harder squeeze makes it more efficient, with strong pulling power at low revs.

faq.q: How does a petrol engine light its fuel?
faq.a: A spark plug in each cylinder makes an electric spark at just the right moment, lighting the squeezed mixture of petrol vapour and air.

faq.q: How does a diesel engine light its fuel without a spark?
faq.a: Squeezing air hard makes it very hot, above 500 degrees Celsius. When diesel is sprayed in as a fine mist, it catches fire by itself.
asks: Do diesel engines have spark plugs?

faq.q: Why do diesel engines use less fuel?
faq.a: They squeeze the air harder, and a higher squeeze turns more of the heat into work. A litre of diesel also holds a little more energy than a litre of petrol.

faq.q: Why do lorries use diesel engines?
faq.a: Diesel engines give strong turning force at low engine speeds and use less fuel, which suits heavy loads and long distances. They are also very hard-wearing.

faq.q: Why are diesel cars less popular now?
faq.a: Diesel exhaust contains more nitrogen oxides and soot, which harm health in cities. Cleaning it needs costly filters and chemical systems, and many cities now charge or limit older diesels.
asks: Are diesel cars bad for the air?

facts: Rudolf Diesel patented his compression-ignition engine in the 1890s.
A litre of diesel holds roughly 10 to 15 percent more energy than a litre of petrol.
Diesel engines squeeze air to roughly a fifteenth to a twentieth of its volume.
